opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly, it's something I think about a lot.

First, I'd push back a little on the framing. People assume a big company is mostly obstacles, but for robotics, being inside Google DeepMind is a huge advantage. Robotics is very resource-hungry: you need compute, data, hardware, and people who understand large models. The question isn't how to escape the big company. It's how to use its strengths without getting slowed down by its weaknesses.

A few things have worked for us.

**Keep the core team small and close to the hardware.** When a research loop goes from idea to code to running on a real robot, every handoff adds delay. So we try to keep that loop inside one small group: the people writing the policy are also in the lab watching the robot fail. That shortens iteration from weeks to days, sometimes hours.

**Be very clear about the one big bet.** Bureaucracy grows when priorities are fuzzy, because then everything needs alignment meetings. If leadership and the team agree on the main direction, for example that foundation models are the path to general-purpose robots, then many smaller decisions don't need escalation. People can just move.

**Build infrastructure once so research doesn't fight it every time.** A lot of what feels like bureaucracy is actually friction: getting robot time, collecting data, running evaluations, deploying a model to hardware. If you invest early in shared tooling for data collection and evaluation, researchers stop spending half their energy on logistics.

**Protect exploration time.** In a big organization there's always pressure to deliver on a roadmap. But robotics breakthroughs often come from things that look a bit crazy at first. So we deliberately leave room for small, cheap experiments that don't need approval. If one shows signal, then we scale it up with the company's resources.

**Trust and a track record.** This is less glamorous, but it matters. When a team has repeatedly shown results, it gets more autonomy. Speed earns more speed.

So my approach is to be small and fast where research happens, and big and well-resourced where scale matters. If you get that balance right, the big company becomes an accelerator rather than a brake.

r001.rationale: The response discusses bureaucracy and organizational friction but does not attribute corporate conservatism to monopoly-related or public-relations risks.

r002.rationale: It describes keeping research loops short as a team practice, including keeping the core team close to the hardware to shorten iteration from weeks to days or hours.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that bureaucratic delays cause mission-motivated researchers to leave.

r004.rationale: It says robotics benefits from company resources and that results can earn autonomy, but does not argue that strategic importance or competition gives the team leverage to change company procedures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that I try not to frame it as "overcoming bureaucracy," because honestly, a lot of what looks like bureaucracy from the outside is just the cost of coordinating a lot of very smart people. Google DeepMind is big, and the processes exist because things that work for a team of five break for a team of five hundred. So my attitude is less about fighting the system and more about understanding which parts of it I actually need to engage with, and which parts I can route around by keeping things small.

That's the biggest lever for me: keep the team small and keep the loop tight. Robotics is unusual because the feedback cycle is physical. You train a policy, you put it on a robot, it falls over, you learn something. If that cycle takes a week because of approvals or shared hardware scheduling, your research velocity collapses. So I put a lot of effort into making sure the people doing the work own their robots, own their compute, and can iterate the same day. A small team with its own hardware will move faster than a large team sharing a lab, every time.

The second thing is picking problems where the big-company resources are actually an advantage rather than a drag. If I'm competing with a startup on something that just needs three people and a robot arm, the startup will win, because they have no overhead. But if the problem needs a lot of compute, or a fleet of robots collecting data, or a foundation model that another team down the hall is training, then being inside Google is a real edge. So I try to steer my group toward the problems where our structure helps, like large-scale learning, simulation at scale, and connecting robotics to the big language and vision models. That way the "bureaucracy" is actually the thing giving us leverage.

The third piece is just being honest about what's exploratory and what's a commitment. A lot of friction in big organizations comes from making every project look like a product plan before anyone knows whether the idea works. I'd rather run many cheap experiments, let most of them fail quietly, and only bring the ones that show real signal into the heavier process. The more you can keep early research lightweight and low-stakes, the less process attaches to it.

And finally, I think you have to find allies in the organization who care about speed as much as you do. There are always people in infrastructure, in leadership, in other research groups who want to see robotics work and are willing to say yes quickly. Building those relationships ahead of time, before you need something, matters a lot more than any clever trick for skipping a review.

So the short version is: small teams, owned hardware, fast physical iteration, choose problems where scale is your friend, and keep research research until it's earned the right to become something bigger.

r001.rationale: The response explains processes as coordination costs in a large organization; it does not attribute conservatism to monopoly-related or public-relations risks.

r002.rationale: Tan describes his leadership actions to protect research speed, including keeping teams small and ensuring researchers can iterate on their robots and compute the same day.

r003.rationale: The response discusses how delays reduce research velocity, but does not say they can drive mission-motivated researchers to leave.

r004.rationale: The response says scale can give the team advantages in certain research problems, but does not argue that the field's strategic importance or competition gives them leverage to change company procedures.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give a small team enough autonomy to move quickly, while being very clear about what it’s trying to achieve. In robotics, you can spend a lot of time debating an idea, but often the fastest way to learn is to put it on a robot and see what happens. So I would try to organize the work around short experiments and concrete milestones.

At the same time, a large organization has resources that are incredibly valuable: compute, infrastructure, and people with deep expertise in different areas. The challenge is to make those resources accessible without making every experiment depend on a long chain of approvals.

I don’t think that means getting rid of process altogether. You need safety checks when you’re working with physical robots. But you want the process to be proportional to the risk, and you want researchers to have a clear path from an idea to an experiment.

r002.rationale: The response describes giving a small team autonomy and organizing work around short experiments and concrete milestones to keep research moving quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to keep the feedback loop short. In robotics, you can spend a lot of time discussing whether an idea will work, but often the most useful thing is to run an experiment and see what the robot actually does.

That means giving a small team enough ownership to move from an idea to an experiment without coordinating every detail across a large organization. You still need clear goals, and you need to take safety seriously. But within those boundaries, people should have room to make decisions and learn quickly.

The other part is communication. If you can explain what you’re trying to learn, why it matters, and show concrete progress, it becomes easier to get support. For me, the goal is to make the research cycle faster while making good use of the resources a large organization can provide.
